title: Visuo-spatial perception deficit in ophthalmological disorders: Visual field extent matters
content:
by Hind Drissi, Marie Jauze, Eloise Perrier, Kenza Takani, Anne Céline Blanc, Armelle Laurens, Amandine Plaza, Jacqueline Jourdan, Julie Ferrotin, Elise Miclo, Lucie Loria, Florence De Saint-Etienne, Carole Malet, Laure Pisella

Objectives

Persons with Visual Impairment (VI) are more at risk to be without academic qualification. This is classically attributed to limited access to visual information, considered difficult due to reduced visual acuity. However, in some cases, visual acuity is preserved but visual field is reduced. Given the importance of visuo-spatial skills in learning, we assessed the accuracy of perceptual visuo-spatial judgements relative to visual field extent and visual acuity to question their respective contribution to the functional repercussions in VI.

Methods

97 patients were administered the elementary visuo-spatial perception (EVSP) test during their clinical assessment. We put a focus on two diseases of our sample: Retinitis Pigmentosa (N = 19) and Albinism (N = 18), with mainly restriction of visual field extent in the former, and visual acuity loss in the latter. In addition, we investigated the correlation between the visuo-spatial performance and these two distinctive factors of VI in the whole sample.

Results

The results indicated higher prevalence of visuo-spatial perception deficit in the whole sample of VI compared to typically developing individuals. Even if most pathologies affect both peripheral and central vision, which makes it complicated to fully disentangle between these two factors, the focus on the Retinitis Pigmentosa and the Albinism groups suggested that visuo-spatial perception is less impacted by a low visual acuity than by peripheral visual field restriction. Additionally, we found that visuospatial perception performance was significantly correlated with visual field extent and not with visual acuity in the whole sample.

Conclusions

Visual field extent matters for visuo-spatial processing and probably for academic achievement. Further investigations are needed to understand how impaired visuo-spatial perceptual skills may explain academic difficulties in VI.
